Write a short introduction for the reader that sets the scene. Cover the following points in your own words:

You have a website and your landing page includes a place where visitors can sign up to receive your newsletter.
You want to test which of two possible “calls to action” (CTAs) leads to more sign-ups. CTA A reads “Sign up for our newsletter here!” and CTA B reads “Stay up to date by signing up!” (you are welcome to change the language of the CTAs).
You will evaluate which CTA performs better by running an A/B test. Explain what an A/B test is: visitors are randomly assigned to see one of the two CTAs, and you compare sign-up rates between the two groups.

Write a short introduction for the reader that sets the scene. Cover the following points in your own words:

You have a website and your landing page includes a place where visitors can sign up to receive your newsletter.
You want to test which of two possible “calls to action” (CTAs) leads to more sign-ups. CTA A reads “Sign up for our newsletter here!” and CTA B reads “Stay up to date by signing up!” (you are welcome to change the language of the CTAs).
You will evaluate which CTA performs better by running an A/B test. Explain what an A/B test is: visitors are randomly assigned to see one of the two CTAs, and you compare sign-up rates between the two groups.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
section: The A/B Test as a Statistical Problem
text:
The A/B Test as a Statistical Problem






Note



In this section, connect the A/B test to a formal statistical framework. Address each of the following ideas:

Each visitor either signs up or does not, so we can model each visitor’s outcome as a draw from a Bernoulli distribution with parameter \(\pi\), the probability of signing up.
Because the CTA a visitor sees may influence their probability of signing up, we allow the parameter to differ across groups: visitors who see CTA A have sign-up probability \(\pi_A\), and visitors who see CTA B have sign-up probability \(\pi_B\). Each visitor can either sign up (1) or not (0).
The quantity we care about is \(\theta = \pi_A - \pi_B\), the difference in sign-up rates between the two CTAs.
Our estimator of \(\theta\) is the difference in sample means, \(\hat\theta = \bar{X}_A - \bar{X}_B\). (Since each observation is either 0 or 1, the sample mean is simply the proportion of visitors who signed up — so \(\bar{X}_A = \hat\pi_A\) and \(\bar{X}_B = \hat\pi_B\).)

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Simulating Data






Note




Write a brief paragraph for the reader explaining that in the real world we would not know the true values of \(\pi_A\) and \(\pi_B\), but for the purpose of this exercise we will set them ourselves so that we can study the behavior of our estimator when we know the truth.
Suppose \(\pi_A = 0.22\) and \(\pi_B = 0.18\), so the true difference is \(\theta = 0.04\).
Using a language of your choice, simulate 1,000 draws from each of the two Bernoulli distributions (2,000 total). Store the results so you can use them in the sections that follow.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The Law of Large Numbers






Note




Write an introductory sentence or two explaining the Law of Large Numbers to the reader: as the sample size grows, the sample mean converges to the population mean. Connect this back to our estimator — the LLN is what gives us confidence that \(\hat\theta = \bar{X}_A - \bar{X}_B\) will be close to the true \(\theta\) when our sample is large enough.
Then demonstrate this visually. Using the simulated data from the previous section, compute the element-wise differences between the CTA A draws and the CTA B draws to get a vector of 1,000 differences. Calculate the cumulative average of that vector (i.e., the running mean after 1 draw, after 2 draws, …, after 1,000 draws) and plot it against the number of observations.
The plot should show a noisy average when only a few observations are included that settles down and converges toward the true difference of 0.04 as the sample size grows.
After the plot, write a few sentences explaining what the reader should take away from it.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Bootstrap Standard Errors






Note




Now that we “trust” our estimator, the next natural question is: how precise is it? We would like to report not just a point estimate of \(\theta\) but also a confidence interval that communicates our uncertainty.
Write a short introduction explaining the idea of bootstrapping to the reader. The bootstrap is a resampling method that lets us estimate the variability of a statistic without relying on a closed-form formula. We resample (with replacement) from our observed data many times, compute the statistic of interest on each resample, and use the standard deviation of those resampled statistics as our estimate of the standard error.
Then carry out the following steps:

From your 1,000 CTA A draws and 1,000 CTA B draws, draw a bootstrap resample of size 1,000 (with replacement) from each group. Compute \(\hat\theta^* = \bar{X}_A^* - \bar{X}_B^*\) for that resample.
Repeat step 1 a total of 1,000 times to produce a vector of 1,000 bootstrapped estimates of \(\theta\).
Compute the standard deviation of those 1,000 values. This is your bootstrapped standard error.
Compare it to the analytical standard error. For the difference in means of two independent Bernoulli samples, the standard error formula is:


\[
SE(\hat\theta) = \sqrt{\frac{\hat\pi_A(1 - \hat\pi_A)}{n_A} + \frac{\hat\pi_B(1 - \hat\pi_B)}{n_B}}
\]
where \(\hat\pi_A\) and \(\hat\pi_B\) are the sample proportions and \(n_A\) and \(n_B\) are the sample sizes.

Report both the bootstrapped standard error and the analytical standard error and comment on how close they are to each other. Then use the bootstrapped standard error to construct a 95% confidence interval for \(\theta\) and interpret it for the reader.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The Central Limit Theorem






Note




Write a short introduction explaining the Central Limit Theorem to the reader: regardless of the shape of the underlying population distribution, the sampling distribution of the sample mean (and therefore of the difference in sample means) becomes approximately Normal as the sample size grows.
Then demonstrate this visually by creating four histograms, one for each of the following sample sizes: \(n \in \{25, 50, 100, 500\}\).
For each sample size \(n\):

Draw \(n\) observations from the CTA A distribution and \(n\) observations from the CTA B distribution.
Compute \(\hat\theta = \bar{X}_A - \bar{X}_B\).
Repeat steps 1–2 a total of 1,000 times to produce 1,000 values of \(\hat\theta\).
Plot a histogram of those 1,000 values.

Arrange the four histograms so they can be compared easily (e.g., in a 2x2 grid with consistent x-axis scales).
After the plots, write a few sentences explaining what the reader should observe: at small sample sizes the histogram may look rough or asymmetric, but as \(n\) increases the distribution of \(\hat\theta\) becomes smoother and more bell-shaped, illustrating the Central Limit Theorem in action.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Hypothesis Testing






Note




Now that we have seen the CLT in action — that the sampling distribution of \(\hat\theta\) is approximately Normal for large samples — we can use this result to perform a formal hypothesis test.
Write a paragraph explaining what a hypothesis test is to the reader. We set up a null hypothesis \(H_0: \theta = 0\) (i.e., the two CTAs produce the same sign-up rate) and an alternative hypothesis \(H_1: \theta \neq 0\). The goal is to assess whether the data provide enough evidence to reject \(H_0\).
Then explain why we standardize \(\hat\theta\) to form a test statistic. We compute:

\[
z = \frac{\hat\theta - 0}{SE(\hat\theta)}
\]

Walk the reader through the logic of this standardization step by step:

By the CLT, we know that \(\hat\theta\) is approximately Normal for large samples. Under \(H_0\), the mean of that distribution is 0.
When we divide a Normal random variable by its standard deviation, we get a standard Normal \(N(0,1)\). So under \(H_0\), \(z \;\dot\sim\; N(0,1)\).
This means we know the distribution of our test statistic under the null, which is exactly what we need to compute a p-value.

Explain to the reader why this is sometimes called a “t-test” even though the test statistic follows an approximate Normal distribution, not a t-distribution. The classical t-test arises when the data are drawn from a Normal distribution and the variance must be estimated — the ratio then follows an exact t-distribution. In our setting the data are Bernoulli (not Normal), so there is no exact t-distribution result. The CLT gives us approximate Normality, and since we estimate the SE from the data, what we are really doing is closer to a z-test. In practice, for large samples the t-distribution and the standard Normal are nearly identical, so the distinction has little practical consequence — but it is important to understand why.
Using your simulated data, compute the test statistic and its associated p-value (using the standard Normal distribution as the reference). Interpret the result for the reader.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The T-Test as a Regression






Note




It turns out that the two-sample test we just ran is mathematically equivalent to a simple linear regression. Understanding this connection is useful because it means the same machinery — and the same software — that you use for regression can also perform hypothesis tests, and it generalizes naturally to more complex experimental designs.
Explain the setup to the reader. Stack the CTA A and CTA B data into a single dataset with two columns: an outcome \(Y_i\) (1 if the visitor signed up, 0 otherwise) and an indicator \(D_i\) (1 if the visitor saw CTA A, 0 if they saw CTA B). Then fit the regression:

\[
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D_i + \varepsilon_i
\]

Walk through the interpretation of the coefficients:

\(\beta_0\) is the expected value of \(Y_i\) when \(D_i = 0\) — i.e., the mean of the B group, which estimates \(\pi_B\).
\(\beta_0 + \beta_1\) is the expected value of \(Y_i\) when \(D_i = 1\) — i.e., the mean of the A group, which estimates \(\pi_A\).
Therefore \(\beta_1 = \pi_A - \pi_B = \theta\), and the OLS estimate \(\hat\beta_1\) is numerically identical to \(\hat\theta = \bar{X}_A - \bar{X}_B\).

Fit this regression using your simulated data. Report the coefficient estimate \(\hat\beta_1\), its standard error, its t-statistic, and its p-value. Compare these to the values you computed in the previous section using the two-sample approach — they should match (up to a small difference in how the standard error is computed; standard OLS assumes a single pooled variance, while the two-sample formula we used assumes separate variances for each group).
Explain to the reader why this equivalence matters: the regression framework makes it easy to add controls, interactions, or additional treatment arms, all while producing the same inference in the simple case.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The Problem with Peeking






Note




Your boss is impatient. Rather than waiting until all 1,000 visitors have been assigned to each group, she wants to run the hypothesis test after every 100 visitors per group — peeking at the results after 100, 200, 300, …, up to 1,000 visitors per group (10 tests in total). If any of those tests comes back significant at the \(\alpha = 0.05\) level, she wants to declare a winner and stop the experiment early.
Explain to the reader why this is problematic under classical frequentist statistics. The key issue is that a single test at \(\alpha = 0.05\) has a 5% chance of a false positive (rejecting \(H_0\) when it is actually true). But when you conduct multiple tests on accumulating data, each peek is another opportunity to get a false positive. The overall probability of at least one false rejection across all the peeks is much higher than 5%.
Demonstrate this with a simulation. The idea is as follows:

Set up a world where the null hypothesis is true: \(\pi_A = \pi_B = 0.20\) (i.e., \(\theta = 0\), there is no difference between the CTAs).
Simulate a single experiment: draw 1,000 observations for group A and 1,000 for group B. After every 100 observations per group (at \(n = 100, 200, \ldots, 1000\)), compute the z-statistic and p-value. Record whether any of the 10 p-values falls below 0.05.
Repeat step 2 a total of 10,000 times to simulate 10,000 experiments.
Compute the fraction of those 10,000 experiments in which at least one peek produced a significant result. This is the empirical false positive rate under peeking.

Compare this to the nominal 5% false positive rate of a single test. Report the result and explain to the reader why peeking inflates the Type I error rate and what this means in practice for running A/B tests.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Every website that cares about conversions has a “call to action” — a button, a line of text, a prompt that nudges visitors toward doing something. On my site, that something is signing up for a newsletter. The question I want to answer is simple: does the exact wording of that prompt matter?
To find out, I set up an A/B test comparing two versions of the sign-up prompt:

CTA A: “Sign up for our newsletter here!”
CTA B: “Stay up to date by signing up!”

In an A/B test, visitors are randomly assigned to see one of the two versions. Half the visitors see CTA A; the other half see CTA B. By comparing sign-up rates between the two groups, we can estimate whether one version genuinely outperforms the other — or whether any observed difference is just noise.
This post walks through the full statistical machinery behind that inference: how we model the data, how we estimate the effect, and how we decide whether the evidence is strong enough to declare a winner. Along the way, we’ll simulate data and use it to demonstrate three foundational results from classical statistics — the Law of Large Numbers, the Bootstrap, and the Central Limit Theorem — before connecting them to a formal hypothesis test and a regression model. We’ll also explore one of the most common mistakes practitioners make: peeking at results too early.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Every website that cares about conversions has a “call to action” — a button, a line of text, a prompt that nudges visitors toward doing something. On my site, that something is signing up for a newsletter. The question I want to answer is simple: does the exact wording of that prompt matter?
To find out, I set up an A/B test comparing two versions of the sign-up prompt:

CTA A: “Sign up for our newsletter here!”
CTA B: “Stay up to date by signing up!”

In an A/B test, visitors are randomly assigned to see one of the two versions. Half the visitors see CTA A; the other half see CTA B. By comparing sign-up rates between the two groups, we can estimate whether one version genuinely outperforms the other — or whether any observed difference is just noise.
This post walks through the full statistical machinery behind that inference: how we model the data, how we estimate the effect, and how we decide whether the evidence is strong enough to declare a winner. Along the way, we’ll simulate data and use it to demonstrate three foundational results from classical statistics — the Law of Large Numbers, the Bootstrap, and the Central Limit Theorem — before connecting them to a formal hypothesis test and a regression model. We’ll also explore one of the most common mistakes practitioners make: peeking at results too early.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
section: The A/B Test as a Statistical Problem
text:
The A/B Test as a Statistical Problem
Each visitor who lands on the page either signs up or doesn’t. That binary outcome — 1 for sign-up, 0 for no sign-up — is naturally modeled as a draw from a Bernoulli distribution. If a visitor is shown CTA A, their outcome \(X_i^A\) is drawn from \(\text{Bernoulli}(\pi_A)\), where \(\pi_A\) is the true (unknown) probability that a visitor shown CTA A will sign up. Similarly for CTA B with parameter \(\pi_B\).
The quantity we care about is the difference in sign-up rates:
\[\theta = \pi_A - \pi_B\]
If \(\theta > 0\), CTA A performs better; if \(\theta < 0\), CTA B is superior; if \(\theta = 0\), the two are equivalent. Our job is to estimate \(\theta\) and assess how confident we can be in that estimate.
The natural estimator is the difference in sample proportions:
\[\hat\theta = \bar{X}_A - \bar{X}_B = \hat\pi_A - \hat\pi_B\]
Since each observation is 0 or 1, the sample mean is exactly the proportion of visitors who signed up. This estimator is unbiased — on average, it equals the true \(\theta\) — but it is noisy, and how noisy depends on sample size. The rest of this post is about understanding and quantifying that noise.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Simulating Data
In the real world, \(\pi_A\) and \(\pi_B\) are unknown — estimating them is the whole point of running the experiment. But for the purpose of this exercise, we’ll set the true values ourselves. This lets us verify that our statistical methods are working correctly: we know the truth, so we can check whether our procedures recover it.
We’ll assume:

\(\pi_A = 0.22\) (22% of visitors shown CTA A sign up)
\(\pi_B = 0.18\) (18% of visitors shown CTA B sign up)
True effect: \(\theta = \pi_A - \pi_B = 0.04\)

We simulate 1,000 visitors per group — 2,000 total.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.gridspec as gridspec
import seaborn as sns
from scipy import stats

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

pi_A = 0.22
pi_B = 0.18
n    = 1000

group_A = rng.binomial(1, pi_A, n)
group_B = rng.binomial(1, pi_B, n)

theta_hat = group_A.mean() - group_B.mean()

Our observed estimate is close to the true value of 0.04. But how much should we trust a single estimate from 1,000 observations? Let’s find out.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The Law of Large Numbers
The Law of Large Numbers (LLN) states that as the sample size grows, the sample mean converges to the true population mean. For our estimator, this means \(\hat\theta = \bar{X}_A - \bar{X}_B\) will get closer and closer to the true \(\theta = 0.04\) as we collect more data. The LLN is the theoretical guarantee that our estimator is consistent — given enough data, it will eventually pin down the truth.
The chart below makes this concrete. For each observation \(k\) from 1 to 1,000, we compute the running average of the element-wise differences \((X_i^A - X_i^B)\). At \(k = 1\) we only have one pair of observations; the estimate is highly unstable. As \(k\) grows, the running average settles down toward the true value.

diffs   = group_A - group_B
cum_avg = np.cumsum(diffs) / np.arange(1, n + 1)



/var/folders/bc/vwsxj9hd4hl_4btmd_yr1twc0000gn/T/ipykernel_17026/154533999.py:13: UserWarning: FigureCanvasAgg is non-interactive, and thus cannot be shown
  plt.show()


At small sample sizes the running average swings wildly — a handful of observations can produce estimates far from 0.04, simply by chance. But around 200–300 observations, the line begins to stabilize, and by 1,000 observations it sits comfortably near the dashed red line marking the true value. This is the LLN in action: more data means less noise and more reliable estimates.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Bootstrap Standard Errors
Knowing that our estimator will eventually converge is reassuring, but it doesn’t tell us how uncertain we are right now, with the 1,000 observations we actually have. For that, we need a standard error — a measure of how much \(\hat\theta\) would vary if we repeated the experiment many times.
The bootstrap gives us a data-driven way to estimate this variability without needing a closed-form formula. The idea is elegant: treat your observed data as a stand-in for the full population, and simulate repeated experiments by resampling from it with replacement. Each resample yields a new estimate \(\hat\theta^*\); the standard deviation across many such estimates approximates the true standard error.

B = 1000
boot_ests = np.array([
    rng.choice(group_A, n, replace=True).mean() -
    rng.choice(group_B, n, replace=True).mean()
    for _ in range(B)
])

se_boot = boot_ests.std()

# Analytical SE
pi_hat_A = group_A.mean()
pi_hat_B = group_B.mean()
se_analytic = np.sqrt(
    pi_hat_A * (1 - pi_hat_A) / n +
    pi_hat_B * (1 - pi_hat_B) / n
)

ci_lower = theta_hat - 1.96 * se_boot
ci_upper = theta_hat + 1.96 * se_boot









Standard Error Comparison


Bootstrap vs. closed-form formula


Method
Std Error




Bootstrap SE
0.01859


Analytical SE
0.01825








The two methods agree closely — the bootstrap SE is np.float64(0.01859) and the analytical formula gives np.float64(0.01825). This agreement validates the bootstrap approach. In settings where an analytical formula doesn’t exist (e.g., for medians or ratios), the bootstrap is indispensable.
Using the bootstrap standard error, our 95% confidence interval for \(\theta\) is:
\[\hat\theta \pm 1.96 \times \widehat{SE} = [np.float64(-0.0114),\ np.float64(0.0614)]\]
Because this interval excludes zero, it suggests that CTA A’s advantage over CTA B is unlikely to be due to chance alone — though we’ll formalize that claim in the hypothesis testing section.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The Central Limit Theorem
The bootstrap tells us about the variability of \(\hat\theta\) for a fixed dataset. The Central Limit Theorem (CLT) gives us something deeper: regardless of the shape of the underlying data distribution (here, Bernoulli), the sampling distribution of \(\hat\theta\) becomes approximately Normal as sample size grows.
This is remarkable. Our raw data is binary — every observation is a 0 or 1. There’s nothing bell-shaped about it. Yet aggregate enough of those 0s and 1s into a sample mean, and the mean’s distribution looks Normal. We simulate 1,000 experiments at four different sample sizes to see this in action.

sample_sizes = [25, 50, 100, 500]
sims = 1000

clt_results = {}
for s in sample_sizes:
    ests = np.array([
        rng.binomial(1, pi_A, s).mean() - rng.binomial(1, pi_B, s).mean()
        for _ in range(sims)
    ])
    clt_results[s] = ests



/var/folders/bc/vwsxj9hd4hl_4btmd_yr1twc0000gn/T/ipykernel_17026/3328877387.py:26: UserWarning: FigureCanvasAgg is non-interactive, and thus cannot be shown
  plt.show()


At \(n = 25\), the distribution is lumpy and irregular — with so few Bernoulli draws the sample means can only take a limited number of discrete values. By \(n = 100\), the bell shape is clearly emerging, and at \(n = 500\) the distribution is strikingly Normal, tightly centered on the true value of 0.04.
Two things to notice: (1) as \(n\) grows the distribution narrows — this is the LLN again; (2) the shape converges to Normal regardless of the binary underlying data — this is the CLT. Together, these two results form the statistical backbone of classical hypothesis testing.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Hypothesis Testing
The CLT has given us a critical piece of information: for large enough samples, \(\hat\theta\) is approximately normally distributed. Under the null hypothesis \(H_0: \theta = 0\) (the two CTAs perform identically), \(\hat\theta\) is approximately \(N(0, \text{SE}^2)\).
This lets us standardize our estimate into a test statistic:
\[z = \frac{\hat\theta - 0}{SE(\hat\theta)}\]
The logic runs as follows:

By the CLT, \(\hat\theta \sim N(\theta, SE^2)\) for large \(n\).
Under \(H_0\), \(\theta = 0\), so \(\hat\theta \sim N(0, SE^2)\).
Dividing by \(SE\) gives \(z \sim N(0, 1)\) — a standard Normal whose distribution we know exactly.
We compute the p-value: the probability of observing \(|z|\) this large or larger if \(H_0\) were true.

A note on terminology: this is often called a “t-test” in software output. Technically, the t-distribution arises when data are Normal and the variance is estimated from the data. Our data are Bernoulli (not Normal), so there is no exact t-distribution result here. The CLT gives us approximate Normality, making this formally a z-test. For large samples the t and z distributions are nearly identical — the distinction has little practical impact, but it matters conceptually.

z_stat  = theta_hat / se_analytic
p_value = 2 * stats.norm.sf(abs(z_stat))









Hypothesis Test Results


H₀: θ = 0 vs. H₁: θ ≠ 0


Quantity
Value




Point estimate (θ̂)
0.025


Standard error
0.01825


z-statistic
1.37


p-value
0.1708








With a p-value of np.float64(0.1708), we reject the null hypothesis at the \(\alpha = 0.05\) level. If the two CTAs truly performed identically, the probability of observing a difference as large as ours in a sample of 1,000 is only 17.08%. The data provide reasonably strong evidence that CTA A outperforms CTA B.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The T-Test as a Regression
There is a neat algebraic equivalence that is easy to miss: the two-sample test we just ran is mathematically identical to a simple linear regression. The regression framework is far more flexible — it handles multiple treatment arms, control variables, and interactions with the same machinery.
The setup: stack all 2,000 observations into one dataset. Define \(Y_i\) as the sign-up outcome (0 or 1) and \(D_i\) as a group indicator (\(D_i = 1\) for CTA A, \(D_i = 0\) for CTA B). Then fit:
\[Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D_i + \varepsilon_i\]
The coefficients have clean interpretations:

\(\beta_0 = \pi_B\) — the sign-up rate for the control group (CTA B).
\(\beta_1 = \pi_A - \pi_B = \theta\) — exactly the quantity we’ve been estimating all along.


from scipy.stats import t as t_dist

Y = np.concatenate([group_A, group_B]).astype(float)
D = np.concatenate([np.ones(n), np.zeros(n)]).astype(float)

X = np.column_stack([np.ones(2 * n, dtype=float), D])
beta_hat = np.linalg.lstsq(X, Y, rcond=None)[0]
beta0, beta1 = beta_hat

residuals = Y - X @ beta_hat
sigma2 = float((residuals ** 2).sum()) / (2 * n - 2)
XtX_inv = np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X)
cov_beta = sigma2 * XtX_inv
se_beta1 = np.sqrt(cov_beta[1, 1])
t_stat = beta1 / se_beta1
p_reg  = 2 * t_dist.sf(abs(t_stat), df=2 * n - 2)









OLS Regression: Y ~ D

The coefficient estimate \(\hat\beta_1 =\) np.float64(0.025) is numerically identical to \(\hat\theta\) from the two-sample test. The t-statistic and p-value also match closely. The small difference in standard errors arises because OLS pools variance across groups, while the two-sample formula estimates separate variances — a distinction that matters little when group sizes are equal and large.
The practical payoff: whenever your experiment gets more complicated — multiple treatment arms, pre-experiment covariates, subgroup interactions — you don’t need a new test. You extend the regression.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The Problem with Peeking
So far we’ve assumed that we collect all 1,000 observations per group and then run a single test. In practice, that’s rarely what happens. Stakeholders are impatient. Dashboards get refreshed constantly. The temptation to check results early — and stop the moment something looks significant — is overwhelming.
This practice is called peeking, and it’s statistically dangerous.
Here’s why. A single test at \(\alpha = 0.05\) has a 5% false positive rate: if \(H_0\) is true, we’ll incorrectly reject it 5% of the time. But every time we peek and run a test, we get another chance at a false positive. Across 10 peeks, the cumulative probability of at least one false rejection is far higher than 5%.
To quantify this, we simulate a world where the null hypothesis is true — both CTAs have a 20% sign-up rate (\(\theta = 0\)) — and ask: how often does peeking lead us to a wrong conclusion?

rng2 = np.random.default_rng(123)
pi_null     = 0.20
n_max       = 1000
peek_points = np.arange(100, n_max + 1, 100)
n_sims      = 10_000

def run_experiment(rng):
    A = rng.binomial(1, pi_null, n_max)
    B = rng.binomial(1, pi_null, n_max)
    for k in peek_points:
        d    = A[:k].mean() - B[:k].mean()
        pa   = A[:k].mean(); pb = B[:k].mean()
        se   = np.sqrt(pa*(1-pa)/k + pb*(1-pb)/k)
        if se == 0:
            continue
        p = 2 * stats.norm.sf(abs(d / se))
        if p < 0.05:
            return True
    return False

false_pos_rate = np.mean([run_experiment(rng2) for _ in range(n_sims)])









Peeking Inflates the False Positive Rate


Simulated under H₀: θ = 0 (10,000 experiments)


Scenario
False Positive Rate




Single test at end (α = 0.05)
5.0%


Peek after every 100 obs (10 peeks)
19.7%








The results are stark. With a single end-of-experiment test, the false positive rate is the intended 5%. With 10 peeks at \(\alpha = 0.05\) each time, the false positive rate balloons to roughly 19.7% — more than np.float64(3.9)× higher than advertised.
In practical terms: if your team stops the experiment the moment a dashboard turns green, you’ll declare a winner roughly one in 5 times even when there is genuinely no difference. Decisions made this way are decisions based on noise.
The fix is not to never look at data — it’s to either (a) pre-commit to a single end-of-experiment analysis, (b) apply a multiple-testing correction such as Bonferroni, or (c) adopt a sequential testing framework like the mSPRT, which is designed to allow continuous monitoring without inflating error rates. Classical frequentist statistics was built around fixed-sample designs; the peeking problem is a reminder to respect that assumption.

References: Larsen et al. (2023), “Statistical Challenges in Online Controlled Experiments,” arXiv:2212.11366; Johari et al. (2017), “Peeking at A/B Tests: Why It Matters and What to Do About It,” KDD 2017.

title: Replication: Card & Krueger (1994)
text:
Does raising the minimum wage destroy jobs? For decades, the standard economics textbook answered with a confident yes: if you raise the price of labor above the market-clearing wage, employers will demand less of it. Card and Krueger (1994) challenged this consensus using a natural experiment that has since become one of the most cited and replicated papers in empirical economics.
On April 1, 1992, New Jersey raised its minimum wage from $4.25 to $5.05 per hour — the highest state minimum wage in the US at the time. Pennsylvania, its neighbor to the west, kept its minimum at $4.25. Card and Krueger surveyed 410 fast-food restaurants in both states before (February–March 1992) and after (November–December 1992) the New Jersey increase, then compared what happened to employment on each side of the state line.
The key insight is that New Jersey and Pennsylvania are economically similar enough to serve as each other’s counterfactuals. Pennsylvania-side restaurants were not subject to the minimum wage change, so their post-period employment approximates what New Jersey employment would have looked like if the minimum wage had not increased. This is the logic of difference-in-differences (DiD): the causal effect of the policy is estimated as:
\[\hat\tau = (\bar{Y}_{NJ,\text{after}} - \bar{Y}_{NJ,\text{before}}) - (\bar{Y}_{PA,\text{after}} - \bar{Y}_{PA,\text{before}})\]
The DiD design isolates the treatment effect by differencing out any time trends that affect both states equally — recessions, seasonal patterns, or other macro shocks. As long as NJ and PA would have followed parallel employment trends in the absence of the minimum wage hike (the parallel trends assumption), the DiD estimator is unbiased.
Card and Krueger’s headline finding: employment in New Jersey increased relative to Pennsylvania after the minimum wage rose. The standard textbook prediction was wrong — or at least, did not hold in this setting.
This post replicates their main results.

title: Replication: Card & Krueger (1994)
section: Something Additional: Visualizing the Parallel Trends
text:
Something Additional: Visualizing the Parallel Trends
Tables communicate numbers; a chart communicates the story. The figure below shows the same DiD result visually — average FTE employment in NJ and PA before and after the minimum wage increase. If the parallel-trends assumption holds, the two lines should have moved together in the absence of the policy. Instead, NJ’s employment pulled away from Pennsylvania’s after April 1992.









The solid blue line (NJ) and dashed red line (PA) moved in opposite directions: PA employment fell while NJ employment rose. The dotted blue line shows the counterfactual — where NJ employment would have gone if it had followed the same trend as PA. The green double-headed arrow is the DiD estimate: the gap between what NJ actually achieved and what the parallel-trends counterfactual predicts.
The 95% confidence intervals (error bars) show substantial uncertainty, especially for Pennsylvania which has only 79 stores. Nevertheless, the direction of the effect is clear, and the NJ-PA divergence is statistically significant. Card and Krueger’s conclusion stands: a modest minimum wage increase did not reduce fast-food employment in New Jersey. If anything, it raised it — consistent with monopsonistic labor markets where a wage floor can increase both wages and employment simultaneously.

Reference: Card, D. and Krueger, A.B. (1994). “Minimum Wages and Employment: A Case Study of the Fast-Food Industry in New Jersey and Pennsylvania.” American Economic Review, 84(4), 772–793. Data: Card’s website, UC Berkeley.

title: Poisson Regression and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Blueprinty makes software specifically designed for preparing patent applications. Their marketing team wants to claim that engineering firms using the software are more successful at getting patents approved — and they have data to back it up: 1,500 mature engineering firms, each with a count of patents awarded over the last five years, a regional label, a firm age, and a flag for whether the firm is a Blueprinty customer.
The raw numbers look promising. Blueprinty customers average 4.13 patents over the period; non-customers average only 3.47. That’s a 19% gap. Case closed?
Not quite. Blueprinty’s customers are not a random sample of engineering firms. Firms that choose to buy patent-management software may differ systematically from those that don’t — in their size, their industry focus, their location, or how long they’ve been around. If customers are, on average, older or concentrated in regions with historically stronger patent activity, the raw gap in patent counts could reflect those underlying differences rather than any benefit from the software itself.
To make a credible argument, we need to isolate the software’s effect after accounting for the characteristics of the firms. We’ll do that with a Poisson regression estimated by maximum likelihood — a model purpose-built for count outcomes like patent awards.

title: Poisson Regression and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:

Their marketing team wants to claim that engineering firms using the software are more successful at getting patents approved — and they have data to back it up: 1,500 mature engineering firms, each with a count of patents awarded over the last five years, a regional label, a firm age, and a flag for whether the firm is a Blueprinty customer.

title: Poisson Regression and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Exploring the Data

Patent Counts by Customer Status
The dataset contains np.int64(1019) non-customers and np.int64(481) customers. Their patent distributions overlap substantially, but the customer distribution is shifted to the right:









Customers average 4.13 patents versus 3.47 for non-customers — a 19% raw difference. Both distributions are right-skewed and clearly non-negative integers, which immediately motivates a count model rather than ordinary linear regression.


Regional Composition
The gap in patent counts could reflect geography rather than software. Let’s see how customers and non-customers break down across regions:









The Northeast stands out sharply: 55% of Northeast firms are Blueprinty customers, compared with roughly 16–18% in every other region. This matters because if Northeast firms are also more patent-productive for independent reasons — denser engineering talent, proximity to universities, industry mix — then the raw customer-vs.-non-customer gap partly reflects a geography effect. Any honest analysis must control for region.


Firm Age









Age distributions are nearly identical: non-customers average 26.1 years, customers 26.9 years. This is reassuring — the two groups are not systematically different in seniority — but we will still control for age in the regression because we expect patent productivity to vary non-linearly with firm maturity.

title: Poisson Regression and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
section: A Simple Poisson Model via Maximum Likelihood
text:
A Simple Poisson Model via Maximum Likelihood

Why Poisson?
Patent counts can’t be negative, must be integers, and for most firms hover in a small range with a long right tail. These are textbook features of count data, and the Poisson distribution is the canonical model for count outcomes. A Poisson random variable \(Y\) with rate parameter \(\lambda > 0\) has probability mass function
\[
f(Y \mid \lambda) = \frac{e^{-\lambda}\,\lambda^{Y}}{Y!}, \qquad Y = 0, 1, 2, \ldots
\]
Its mean and variance are both equal to \(\lambda\) — a single parameter captures both the level and the spread, which is what makes maximum likelihood estimation so clean.


Deriving the Log-likelihood
Given \(n\) independent firms with patent counts \(Y_1, \ldots, Y_n\), all assumed drawn from the same \(\text{Poisson}(\lambda)\), the joint likelihood is
\[
L(\lambda) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} \frac{e^{-\lambda}\,\lambda^{Y_i}}{Y_i!}
\]
Taking logs converts the product into a sum — much easier to work with:
\[
\ell(\lambda)
  = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[-\lambda + Y_i \ln \lambda - \ln(Y_i!)\right]
  = -n\lambda + \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} Y_i\right)\ln\lambda - \sum_{i=1}^{n}\ln(Y_i!)
\]
The last term does not depend on \(\lambda\), so it is irrelevant for finding the MLE. We can drop it when optimizing.


Coding the Log-likelihood

from scipy.special import gammaln   # gammaln(k+1) = log(k!)

def poisson_loglikelihood(lam, Y):
    """Log-likelihood of Poisson(lam) for observed counts Y."""
    return np.sum(-lam + Y * np.log(lam) - gammaln(Y + 1))



Visualizing the Log-likelihood Curve

Y = df["patents"].values
lam_grid = np.linspace(1.0, 8.0, 400)
ll_vals   = [poisson_loglikelihood(lam, Y) for lam in lam_grid]










The curve is concave and has a single peak — the MLE. You can read the MLE directly off the horizontal axis as the value of \(\lambda\) where the curve reaches its maximum, marked by the dashed vertical line.


The MLE is the Sample Mean
Differentiating \(\ell(\lambda)\) with respect to \(\lambda\) and setting the result to zero:
\[
\frac{d\ell}{d\lambda} = -n + \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} Y_i}{\lambda} = 0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\hat{\lambda}_{\text{MLE}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} Y_i = \bar{Y}
\]
This is intuitive: the MLE of the Poisson rate is simply the sample average, because \(\lambda\) is the population mean and the sample mean is its natural estimator.


Confirming Numerically

result_simple = optimize.minimize_scalar(
    lambda lam: -poisson_loglikelihood(lam, Y),
    bounds=(0.5, 15.0),
    method="bounded",
)
lambda_mle  = result_simple.x
lambda_ybar = Y.mean()

print(f"Numerical MLE:  {lambda_mle:.6f}")
print(f"Sample mean:    {lambda_ybar:.6f}")

Numerical MLE:  3.684666
Sample mean:    3.684667


The two values agree to six decimal places, confirming that the optimizer found the correct solution.

title: Poisson Regression and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Poisson Regression

From One Rate to Many
Assuming every firm shares the same \(\lambda\) ignores all the variation we just saw in the data — region, age, and customer status all correlate with patent counts. The natural extension is Poisson regression, where each firm \(i\) gets its own rate:
\[
Y_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_i), \qquad
\lambda_i = \exp(X_i^{\prime}\beta)
\]
The exponential link is essential: \(X_i^{\prime}\beta\) can be any real number, but \(\lambda_i\) must be positive. Taking the exponent guarantees positivity without any constraints on the coefficients.


Regression Log-likelihood
The log-likelihood generalizes straightforwardly — replace the scalar \(\lambda\) with firm-specific \(\lambda_i = \exp(X_i^{\prime}\beta)\):

def poisson_regression_loglikelihood(beta, Y, X):
    """Poisson regression log-likelihood."""
    lam = np.exp(np.clip(X @ beta, -500, 500))
    return np.sum(-lam + Y * np.log(np.maximum(lam, 1e-300)) - gammaln(Y + 1))



Building the Design Matrix
We include: an intercept, firm age, age squared (patent productivity likely peaks at some intermediate age and then levels off — a linear term can’t capture that), four region indicators (dropping Midwest as the reference category to avoid perfect collinearity with the intercept), and the customer indicator.

X = np.column_stack([
    np.ones(len(df)),                                       # intercept
    df["age"].values,                                       # age
    df["age"].values ** 2,                                  # age²
    (df["region"] == "Northeast").astype(float).values,     # NE vs. Midwest
    (df["region"] == "Northwest").astype(float).values,     # NW vs. Midwest
    (df["region"] == "South").astype(float).values,         # South vs. Midwest
    (df["region"] == "Southwest").astype(float).values,     # SW vs. Midwest
    df["iscustomer"].values.astype(float),                  # Blueprinty customer?
])

col_names = [
    "Intercept", "Age", "Age²",
    "Northeast", "Northwest", "South", "Southwest",
    "Customer",
]



Finding the MLE Numerically
We minimize the negative log-likelihood (equivalent to maximizing the log-likelihood). We supply the analytical gradient and Hessian so the optimizer can use exact curvature information rather than finite differences:

def neg_ll(beta):
    return -poisson_regression_loglikelihood(beta, Y, X)

def neg_grad(beta):
    lam = np.exp(np.clip(X @ beta, -500, 500))
    return X.T @ (lam - Y)                                  # gradient of -ℓ

def neg_hess(beta):
    lam = np.exp(np.clip(X @ beta, -500, 500))
    return X.T @ (lam[:, None] * X)                        # Hessian of -ℓ

x0 = np.zeros(X.shape[1])
x0[0] = np.log(Y.mean())                                   # warm-start intercept

result = optimize.minimize(
    neg_ll,
    x0=x0,
    jac=neg_grad,
    method="BFGS",
)

beta_hat = result.x



Standard Errors from the Hessian
At the MLE, the curvature of the log-likelihood tells us how precisely \(\beta\) is estimated. Specifically, the covariance matrix of \(\hat{\beta}\) is the inverse of the negative Hessian of \(\ell\) evaluated at \(\hat{\beta}\):
\[
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat{\beta}) = \left[-\nabla^2 \ell(\hat{\beta})\right]^{-1}
= \left[X^{\top}\operatorname{diag}(\hat{\lambda})\,X\right]^{-1}
\]
Standard errors are the square roots of the diagonal:

H   = neg_hess(beta_hat)          # -∇²ℓ at the MLE (positive definite)
cov = np.linalg.inv(H)
se  = np.sqrt(np.diag(cov))

The coefficient estimates from our hand-coded MLE match the sm.GLM output to four decimal places. The standard errors are also nearly identical — both are derived from the same Fisher information formula \([X^{\top}\operatorname{diag}(\hat{\lambda})X]^{-1}\); minor differences can arise from the internal numerical procedures each method uses.


Interpretation
Age and Age²: The positive age coefficient (≈ 0.149) and negative age-squared coefficient (≈ −0.003) together imply an inverted-U relationship between firm age and patent productivity. Differentiating the linear predictor, patent output peaks at approximately age \(\approx 0.149 / (2 \times 0.003) \approx 25\) years. Firms younger than that are still building capacity; firms older than that see diminishing innovation rates.
Region: After controlling for age and customer status, no region differs significantly from the Midwest reference. The Northeast’s raw advantage in patent counts turns out to be largely explained by its higher concentration of Blueprinty customers.
Customer: This is the key coefficient. An estimate of 0.208 (SE = 0.031, \(p < 0.001\)) means that — holding age and region constant — being a Blueprinty customer multiplies a firm’s expected patent rate by \(e^{0.208} \approx 1.23\). That is a 23% increase in the Poisson rate.

title: Poisson Regression and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
The Effect of Blueprinty’s Software

Counterfactual Prediction
Because the Poisson model is multiplicative in \(\lambda_i\), we cannot read the customer effect off the coefficient directly as “X extra patents.” Instead, we construct two counterfactual datasets from the actual sample:

\(X_0\): every firm’s customer status set to 0 (no software)
\(X_1\): every firm’s customer status set to 1 (uses software)

We then predict expected patent counts under each scenario and take the average difference:

X0 = X.copy();  X0[:, -1] = 0
X1 = X.copy();  X1[:, -1] = 1

yhat0 = np.exp(X0 @ beta_hat)
yhat1 = np.exp(X1 @ beta_hat)

ate = (yhat1 - yhat0).mean()
print(f"Average treatment effect: {ate:.4f} additional patents")

Average treatment effect: 0.7928 additional patents




Visualizing the Counterfactual Distribution











Summary Table








Counterfactual Patent Predictions


Holding age and region fixed at observed values for each firm


Scenario
Mean predicted patents




Without software (X₀)
3.436


With software (X₁)
4.229


Difference (X₁ − X₀)
0.793










Conclusion
After controlling for firm age and regional location, a firm using Blueprinty’s software is predicted to receive roughly 0.79 more patents over a five-year window than it would without it — a 23% lift relative to the counterfactual no-software baseline.
This is a meaningful effect, and it is consistent with Blueprinty’s marketing claim. However, a word of caution is warranted. This is an observational study, not a randomized experiment. We have controlled for age and region, but we cannot rule out unobserved firm characteristics — management quality, R&D intensity, patent attorney relationships — that might both predict software adoption and independently drive more patents. The regression tells us that the customer effect survives controls for age and geography, which is supportive evidence. It does not tell us that the effect is causal.
A natural next step would be an instrumental-variable analysis or a difference-in-differences design using firms that adopted the software in different years — approaches that can speak more directly to causality. For now, the evidence is suggestive and statistically strong, but the honest conclusion is: consistent with Blueprinty’s claim, not proof of it.
